stem: When reviewing post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease (PTLD) presentation during evaluation teaching, which statement aligns with standard references?

options.text: PTLD always presents with isolated graft tenderness and fever
Asymptomatic PTLD never occurs in transplant recipients
PTLD presentation is limited to skin lesions only

explanation.rationale_correct: Clinical presentation of PTLD is noted to include a range of symptoms, and PTLD may be asymptomatic.

rationale_incorrect.B: Presentation is variable and may be asymptomatic rather than always presenting with classic graft tenderness and fever.
rationale_incorrect.C: Asymptomatic PTLD is explicitly noted as possible.
rationale_incorrect.D: PTLD may involve multiple organ systems and presentations beyond skin lesions alone.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → PTLD → 3. Clinical presentation

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 6 → PTLD → 3. Clinical presentation (PTLD may be asymptomatic); PDF p. 281 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Asymptomatic-PTLD recall angle distinct from PTLD combo distractor use (cctc-2111) and extranodal epidemiology (cctc-2112); anchor verified on Cupples p. 281.

stem: A transplant recipient with abdominal pain and peritoneal signs is being evaluated for possible PTLD. Which gastrointestinal complication aligns with standard PTLD presentation references?

options.text: GI tract involvement with intestinal perforation and peritonitis
PTLD never involves the gastrointestinal tract
Intestinal perforation excludes PTLD from the differential
GI involvement occurs only as asymptomatic colon polyps without peritoneal signs

explanation.rationale_correct: PTLD clinical presentation may include GI tract involvement with intestinal perforation and peritonitis, among other systemic and localizing symptoms.

rationale_incorrect.B: GI tract involvement is specifically listed in PTLD presentation.
rationale_incorrect.C: Intestinal perforation and peritonitis are cited complications rather than excluding PTLD.
rationale_incorrect.D: GI involvement may present with perforation and peritonitis rather than only silent polyps.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → PTLD → 3. Clinical presentation → j.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: GI tract involvement: intestinal perforation and peritonitis

references.locator: Ch. 6 → PTLD → 3.j. (GI tract involvement: intestinal perforation and peritonitis); PDF p. 281 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. GI-perforation presentation angle distinct from extranodal epidemiology (cctc-2112) and PTLD symptom list (cctc-2111); anchor verified on Cupples p. 281.

stem: During pretransplant evaluation of bone-health planning, which treatment option aligns with standard references for osteopenia or osteoporosis?

options.text: Hormone replacement therapy in carefully selected patients
Hormone replacement therapy is universally required for all transplant candidates
No pharmacologic or hormonal options exist for bone loss
Hormone therapy is permanently contraindicated in every candidate

explanation.rationale_correct: Bone-health treatment options include hormone replacement therapy in carefully selected patients, along with calcium and vitamin D, bisphosphonates, calcitonin, denosumab, and exercise.

rationale_incorrect.B: Hormone replacement is an option in carefully selected patients rather than a universal requirement.
rationale_incorrect.C: Multiple pharmacologic bone therapies are listed when indicated.
rationale_incorrect.D: Hormone replacement may be considered in selected patients rather than being universally contraindicated.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → Preserve bone health → Prevent or treat osteopenia/osteoporosis → e.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Hormone replacement therapy in carefully selected patients

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 6 → Preserve bone health → 2.e. (hormone replacement therapy in carefully selected patients); PDF p. 322 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. HRT bone-therapy angle distinct from baseline DEXA screening (cctc-2107) and denosumab post-transplant item (cctc-3121); anchor verified on Cupples p. 322.

stem: When counseling a seronegative recipient about Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) risk after transplantation, which outcome spectrum aligns with standard references?

options.text: Sequelae may range from a mononucleosis-like syndrome to post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease (PTLD)
EBV infection causes only mild cold symptoms and never progresses
PTLD is unrelated to EBV infection

explanation.rationale_correct: Effects of EBV infection include sequelae ranging from a mononucleosis-like syndrome to post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease, particularly relevant in primary infection during the early post-transplant period.

rationale_incorrect.B: EBV sequelae may be more severe than mild cold symptoms and can include PTLD.
rationale_incorrect.C: PTLD is among the cited sequelae of EBV infection.
rationale_incorrect.D: Mononucleosis-like illness is on the spectrum that may progress to PTLD rather than excluding it.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 5, Infectious Diseases → Epstein-Barr virus → 2. Incidence → c.i. → ii.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: sequelae of EBV infection range from a mononucleosis-like syndrome to posttransplant lymphoproliferative disease

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 5 → Epstein-Barr virus → 2.c.ii. (sequelae from mononucleosis-like syndrome to PTLD); PDF p. 198 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).
